q: An owner wants an entire neighborhood's zoning district changed from residential to commercial. In a New York town, which body has the power to amend the zoning ordinance and map?
options: The town board
The zoning board of appeals
The planning board
The building inspector
explanation: Adopting and amending zoning is a legislative act of the town board (city council or village board of trustees). The ZBA grants variances and interprets the ordinance; it cannot rezone.

q: In a New York village, which elected body adopts the zoning law and the village budget?
options: The zoning board of appeals
The planning board
The board of trustees
The board of assessment review
explanation: A village's legislative body is its board of trustees, which adopts local laws including zoning, plus the budget and tax rate. Appointed boards such as the planning board and ZBA do not.

q: Which statement about a town planning board is accurate?
options: Its members are elected by town voters, and it grants use and area variances
Its members are appointed by the town board, and it reviews subdivision plats
Its members are appointed by the governor, and it collects town property taxes
Its members are elected by town voters, and it adopts the annual town budget
explanation: Planning board members are appointed by the legislative body. The board performs authorized land-use review such as subdivision plats and site plans, and advises on the comprehensive plan.

q: A company wants to build an office building on a lot where offices are a permitted use. The town requires review of the parking layout, lighting, drainage and landscaping. This is:
options: A use variance hearing before the zoning board of appeals
A rezoning before the town board
A certificate of occupancy inspection
Site plan review, typically by the planning board
explanation: Site plan review examines how a permitted use is laid out on the parcel: parking, access, lighting, drainage and landscaping. No variance is needed because the use is allowed.

q: A building inspector denies a permit because he interprets a proposed garage apartment as a prohibited second dwelling. The owner believes the ordinance allows it. Where does the owner first appeal the interpretation?
options: The town board of assessment review
The County Clerk
The Department of State
The zoning board of appeals
explanation: The ZBA hears appeals from orders, interpretations and determinations of the administrative official charged with enforcing the zoning ordinance. It acts as the ordinance's interpreter.

q: Which description of a zoning board of appeals is most accurate?
options: A legislative body that rewrites the zoning map when owners request it
A quasi-judicial body that applies legal standards to appeals and variances
An elected body that sets the tax rate and adopts the budget
An advisory body whose decisions are never binding on applicants
explanation: The ZBA is administrative and quasi-judicial: it decides appeals, interpretations and variance requests under statutory standards. Rezoning is legislative and belongs to the governing board.

q: A property owner in a designated design district wants to replace a storefront facade and add a large sign. Which local body typically reviews exterior appearance, signs and fences where established?
options: The architectural review board
The board of assessment review
The conservation advisory council
The county health department
explanation: An architectural review board reviews the effect of new construction or alterations on the surrounding area, especially exteriors, signs and fences. Its approval is separate from zoning and building-code compliance.
citation: NY Town Law; NY Village Law (local architectural review law)

q: What is the primary role of a municipal conservation advisory council?
options: To issue building permits for new homes proposed near wetlands
To grant area and use variances for building in environmental zones
To study and advise on the community's natural resources and open space
To set assessed values for undeveloped open land on the tax roll
explanation: A conservation advisory council is an appointed body that inventories and advises on natural resources and open space. It does not issue building permits, grant variances, or replace a DEC wetland permit.

q: A buyer's agent wants to confirm that a finished basement was built with permits and passed inspection. Which local office should be contacted?
options: The building department or code enforcement office
The receiver of taxes or the town assessor's office
The zoning board of appeals or the planning board
The town board clerk's election office
explanation: The building department issues building permits, conducts inspections, issues certificates of occupancy/completion and handles violations. It is the gatekeeper for construction activity.
citation: NY Executive Law Article 18; local building code

q: A homeowner complains that her property tax bill is too high and asks who set the tax rate. Which statement is correct?
options: The assessor sets both the assessed value and the tax rate
The receiver of taxes sets both the assessed value and the tax rate
The assessor values property; the legislative body sets the levy and tax rate
The planning board sets the tax rate as part of the master plan
explanation: The assessor estimates value for the assessment roll. The governing body adopts the budget and tax levy, from which the rate is derived, and the receiver of taxes collects. These roles are separate.

q: A buyer is purchasing a rural lot with no public sewer. Which agency typically must approve the design of a new septic system?
options: The zoning board of appeals
The county health department
The architectural review board
The town assessor
explanation: Septic system design approval is typically handled by the county (or state) health department under sanitary code standards, not by zoning or design boards.
citation: NY Public Health Law; county sanitary code

q: A town proposes rezoning a parcel within 500 feet of a state highway. Before final action, New York law generally requires the town to:
options: Obtain approval from the State Department of Transportation
Hold a referendum of all town voters
Obtain a positive declaration under SEQR
Refer the proposal to the county planning agency for review
explanation: Certain zoning actions affecting property within 500 feet of a municipal boundary, state or county road, park or other listed facilities must be referred to the county planning agency. If the county recommends disapproval or modification, the local board can act contrary to it only by a vote of a majority plus one of all its members.

q: An owner of a designated landmark building in New York City wants to replace its original windows. Which agency must approve the work?
options: The Board of Standards and Appeals
The City Planning Commission
The local community board
The Landmarks Preservation Commission
explanation: NYC's Landmarks Preservation Commission designates landmarks and historic districts and regulates alterations to designated properties. Historic age alone is not landmark status.
citation: NYC Administrative Code § 25-301 et seq. (Landmarks Law)

q: In New York City, which agency issues building permits and certificates of occupancy and enforces the construction codes?
options: The City Planning Commission
The Department of Buildings
The Board of Standards and Appeals
The Department of Finance
explanation: The NYC Department of Buildings issues permits and COs, inspects work and enforces the construction codes and Zoning Resolution. CPC handles planning/zoning changes; BSA grants variances.
citation: NYC Charter Chapter 26; NYC Construction Codes

q: An owner in New York City needs a zoning variance for a building that cannot meet a setback requirement because of the lot's irregular shape. Which body decides the variance?
options: The Board of Standards and Appeals
The City Planning Commission
The NYC Department of Buildings
The local community board
explanation: In NYC, the Board of Standards and Appeals grants zoning variances and certain special permits and hears appeals from Department of Buildings determinations. It plays the role a ZBA plays elsewhere.

q: In New York City, which body votes on zoning map amendments during ULURP, after the community board and borough president have made recommendations?
options: The Board of Standards and Appeals
The Department of Buildings
The City Planning Commission
The Landmarks Preservation Commission
explanation: Under ULURP, the City Planning Commission holds a hearing and votes after the community board and borough president review. Its approvals then go to the City Council for review.

q: Which is the correct order of review under NYC's Uniform Land Use Review Procedure (ULURP) after an application is certified complete?
options: Community board, borough president, City Planning Commission, City Council
Borough president, community board, City Council, City Planning Commission
City Planning Commission, City Council, community board, borough president
Community board, City Council, borough president, City Planning Commission
explanation: ULURP runs: Department of City Planning certifies the application, then community board review, borough president review, City Planning Commission vote, and City Council review, with a possible mayoral veto.

q: Under ULURP, a community board votes to disapprove a proposed rezoning. What is the effect?
options: The application is automatically denied and may not proceed
The application must be refiled with the Board of Standards and Appeals
The recommendation is advisory; the application continues to later review stages
The rezoning may proceed only if the mayor overrides the board
explanation: Community board and borough president recommendations are advisory. Binding decisions are made by the City Planning Commission and the City Council.

q: Under ULURP, how long does the community board have to hold a public hearing and submit its recommendation after receiving a certified application?
options: 30 days
60 days
50 days
90 days
explanation: The community board has 60 days, the borough president 30 days, the City Planning Commission 60 days, and the City Council 50 days. Don't mix up the 30-day borough president period.

q: Before a town zoning board of appeals decides a variance application, Town Law requires the board to:
options: Obtain the town board's written consent
Get approval from the county clerk
Get a certificate of occupancy for the parcel
Hold a public hearing after giving public notice
explanation: The ZBA must fix a time for a public hearing, give public notice (including newspaper publication), and let interested parties be heard before deciding.

q: A neighbor believes the town ZBA wrongly granted a use variance next door. How is the decision generally challenged in court?
options: An Article 78 proceeding, which may be brought at any time within six years after the decision
An appeal to the town board, which may reverse any decision of the zoning board of appeals
A complaint to the Department of State, which may revoke the variance
An Article 78 proceeding, generally within 30 days after the decision is filed with the town clerk
explanation: ZBA decisions are reviewed by an Article 78 proceeding in State Supreme Court. Town Law sets a short deadline: 30 days after the decision is filed in the town clerk's office. The town board does not sit as an appeals body over the ZBA.

q: In an Article 78 proceeding challenging a planning board decision, what does the court generally decide?
options: Whether the court itself would have voted the same way after holding a new hearing
Whether the decision was illegal, arbitrary and capricious, or lacked a rational basis
Whether the applicant's project would be the most profitable use of the property
Whether a majority of residents support the planning board's decision
explanation: Article 78 review is deferential. The court asks whether the agency acted lawfully and rationally (not arbitrarily or capriciously) and does not substitute its own judgment or rehear the application from scratch.

q: A house sits inside an incorporated village that has adopted its own zoning law. The surrounding town also has a zoning law. Which zoning rules govern the house?
options: The town's law, because the village lies inside the town
The village's law; town zoning does not reach village land
Whichever of the two laws is stricter on each point
The county's law, which overrides town and village rules
explanation: A town's zoning power covers only the territory outside its incorporated villages, so a village zones its own land. Being geographically inside the town does not subject village land to town zoning, and counties generally do not zone in New York.

q: In a New York town, the town supervisor is best described as:
options: An appointed manager who has no vote on the town board
The chair of the planning board, named by the governor
The official who values parcels for the assessment roll
The presiding officer and a voting member of the town board
explanation: The town board is made up of the elected supervisor and the town council members; the supervisor presides and votes. Valuing parcels is the assessor's job, and planning board members are appointed locally, not by the governor.

q: A town board wants to appoint one of its own council members to fill a vacancy on the town zoning board of appeals. Is this allowed?
options: No; a town board member is ineligible to serve on the ZBA
Yes, if the member abstains on any variance votes
Yes, as long as the ZBA keeps five members in total
Yes, but only if the member also serves as ZBA chair
explanation: Town Law bars a member of the town board from serving on the zoning board of appeals. Keeping the legislative body off the quasi-judicial appeals board keeps the policy maker separate from the body that applies the law to individual cases.

q: A town planning board member did not complete the required annual training, and the town board did not waive it. What is the legal effect?
options: Every decision the member voted on that year becomes void
The member must step down at once and repay any stipend
Board decisions stand, but the member may be denied reappointment
The planning board loses its power to review subdivisions
explanation: Planning board members must complete at least 4 hours of training a year unless the town board waives or modifies it. Missing it can make a member ineligible for reappointment, but the statute says no board decision is voided because of it.

q: During site plan review, a planning board discovers the applicant's proposed use is not permitted in the zoning district. Short of a rezoning, where must the applicant seek relief?
options: The planning board, which can waive the use restriction
The zoning board of appeals, through a use variance
The building inspector, through a conditional permit
The county planning agency, through a use approval
explanation: Only the ZBA grants use variances (the town board could instead rezone). A planning board reviews site layout for uses the zoning allows; it cannot authorize a use the zoning prohibits.

q: Which statement about a town comprehensive plan is accurate?
options: The ZBA adopts it and uses it as its variance standard
The county clerk records it, and it then binds only buyers
The planning board adopts it, and it overrides the zoning law
The town board adopts it, and zoning must be consistent with it
explanation: The town board adopts the comprehensive plan, though it may have the planning board prepare it, and town land-use regulations must be in accordance with the plan. The planning board advises and drafts; it does not adopt the plan.

q: A developer proposes grouping 20 homes on smaller lots in one corner of a 60-acre tract, preserving the rest as permanent open space, with no more homes than a conventional layout would allow. This is:
options: Cluster development, approved by the planning board as authorized by the town board
Spot zoning, which the ZBA must approve as a use variance for the reduced lot size
A realty subdivision, which only the county health department may approve as drawn
Inclusionary zoning, which the building department approves when issuing permits
explanation: Cluster development lets the planning board, when the town board has authorized it, modify lot sizes so homes are grouped and open space preserved, without exceeding the unit count of a conventional subdivision. No use variance is needed because the use stays residential.

q: An owner in a village wins architectural review board approval for a new storefront facade. Can the owner start construction right away?
options: Yes, because ARB approval includes building code review
Yes, unless a neighbor objects within the next 30 days
No; a building permit is still needed from code enforcement
No; the county must also approve every facade change
explanation: Architectural review covers appearance; structural and code compliance is a separate building-department approval. One office's approval does not approve another office's subject matter.
citation: NYS Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code, 19 NYCRR Part 1203; local ARB law

q: A town's conservation advisory council finishes an inventory and map of the town's open areas, and the town board accepts it as the official open space index. What may the town board now do?
options: Let the council issue wetland permits in place of DEC
Redesignate the council as a conservation board
Give the council power to grant area variances
Let the council adopt zoning changes without a hearing
explanation: Once the open space index is accepted, the legislative body may redesignate the CAC as a conservation board, which must receive and report on applications affecting listed open areas. It remains advisory: it cannot issue DEC permits, grant variances or rezone.

q: A member of a town conservation advisory council tells a buyer that the soggy back acre of a lot "isn't a regulated wetland." The buyer's agent should recommend that the buyer:
options: Rely on the statement, since the council regulates wetlands
Get the council's view in a signed letter and rely on that
Ask the assessor to reclassify the acre as dry upland
Obtain a written jurisdictional determination from DEC
explanation: A CAC studies and advises; an informal remark from a member is not a determination by the agency with wetland jurisdiction. The buyer needs a written determination from DEC (plus any local wetland regulator); a signed letter from the council still lacks that authority.

q: A village has opted out of administering and enforcing the New York State Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code. Who then enforces the code there?
options: The county, or the Department of State if the county also opts out
No one, because opting out exempts the village from the code
The village zoning board of appeals, as part of its variances
The county health department, along with its septic reviews
explanation: A city, town or village may opt out of enforcing the Uniform Code, but the code still applies: the county takes over, and if the county also declines, the Department of State enforces it. Opting out shifts enforcement; it never exempts buildings from the code.

q: A buyer's agent checks the town building department file for a listing. It shows a permit issued in 2019 for a rear deck, but no final inspection or certificate. What does this most likely mean?
options: The deck is legal because the permit was issued
The permit is still open; the work was never signed off
The deck is grandfathered because the permit is old
The assessor's records will show it passed inspection
explanation: Issuing a permit authorizes work to start; the final inspection and certificate show it was completed in compliance. An open permit is a common closing problem the seller usually must close out, and age alone does not grandfather unapproved work.

q: Before closing, the buyer's attorney wants to confirm the seller has paid this year's town and county property taxes. Which local office keeps that payment record?
options: The town assessor, who values each parcel
The board of assessment review, which hears grievances
The receiver of taxes, who collects the tax payments
The county clerk, who records deeds and mortgages
explanation: The receiver of taxes (tax collector or treasurer in some places) bills and collects taxes and keeps payment records. The assessor sets assessed values and the board of assessment review hears grievances; neither tracks whether a bill was paid.
citation: Real Property Tax Law Article 9; local tax collection practice

q: The assessor's property record card for a house lists a "basement apartment." The seller says this proves the apartment is legal. Is the seller right?
options: Yes; the assessor approves every dwelling unit it lists
Yes; any unit taxed for over ten years is legal by default
No; only the county clerk can confirm that a unit is legal
No; legality turns on zoning and the building department file
explanation: The assessor records physical characteristics for valuation; listing a unit does not approve it. Whether an apartment is legal depends on zoning and on permits and a certificate of occupancy from the building department.
citation: Real Property Tax Law (assessment function); 19 NYCRR Part 1203

q: Each of the following sites lies within 500 feet of a county road. Which local action would NOT require referral to the county planning agency under GML §239-m?
options: Issuing a building permit for a house that meets zoning
Granting an area variance for a reduced side setback
Approving a site plan for a new medical office building
Issuing a special use permit for a drive-through bank
explanation: Section 239-m covers zoning and planning actions such as zoning amendments, special use permits, site plan approvals and use or area variances. A routine building permit for a conforming house is not one of the listed actions, so it is not referred.

q: Which location would make a town's proposed special use permit subject to county planning referral under GML §239-m?
options: Within 500 feet of a public elementary school
Within 500 feet of an adjoining town's boundary
Within 1,000 feet of a house of worship
Within 500 feet of a private golf course
explanation: Referral is triggered by land within 500 feet of features such as a municipal boundary, a county or state park, a county or state road, county-owned drainage, county or state land holding a public building, or a farm in an agricultural district. Schools, churches and private recreation sites are not on the list.

q: The county planning agency recommends disapproval of a use variance referred by a five-member town ZBA. What is the minimum number of ZBA votes needed to grant the variance anyway?
options: 3 votes, a simple majority of the board
3 votes of whichever members attend
4 votes, a majority plus one of all members
5 votes, because the action must be unanimous
explanation: To act contrary to a county recommendation of disapproval or modification, the board needs a majority plus one of all its members, and it must give its reasons in the report of final action filed with the county within 30 days. Majority of 5 = 3; 3 + 1 = 4. Counting only the members present is the trap.

q: A town planning board refers a site plan to the county planning agency under GML §239-m. Thirty days pass after the county received the full statement, and the county has sent no recommendation. The planning board may:
options: Not act until the county formally responds
Act only by a majority plus one of its members
Treat the county's silence as a disapproval
Take final action without the county's report
explanation: The county has 30 days from receiving a full statement (or a longer agreed period) to respond. If it does not, the referring board may act without the report; silence is not a disapproval, so the majority-plus-one vote is not triggered.

q: A buyer plans to build a home on a rural lot with a private well and a new septic system. Under State Health Department standards, the absorption field must generally be at least how far from the well?
options: 100 feet
25 feet
50 feet
200 feet
explanation: Appendix 75-A requires 100 feet between a well and an absorption field. 50 feet is the separation for the septic tank, and 200 feet applies when the field sits upgrade in the drainage path to the well; county health departments may require more.

q: A buyer of a house served by a private well wants a reliable water quality test before the contingency expires. The most dependable approach is to:
options: Rely on the seller's answers about the well on the PCDS
Have a State Health Department ELAP-certified lab test a sample
Ask the town building department for its file on the well
Use a store-bought home test kit and keep the printed results
explanation: Drinking water results are reliable when a lab certified by the NYS Department of Health's Environmental Laboratory Approval Program analyzes a properly taken sample; the county health department can help interpret them. A seller's disclosure and home kits are not lab-certified results.

q: A Type I action needs a town board rezoning, a planning board site plan approval and a DEC permit. If the involved agencies cannot agree within 30 days on which will be lead agency under SEQR, who designates it?
options: The county planning agency
The applicant, by written election
The Commissioner of DEC
The New York Secretary of State
explanation: In coordinated review the involved agencies have 30 days to agree on a lead agency; if they cannot, any involved agency or the project sponsor may ask the DEC Commissioner, who then designates one. The applicant can request a designation but does not choose the lead agency, and the county agency's role is the separate §239-m referral.

q: A town's conservation advisory council wants to comment during SEQR review of a large subdivision, but it has no power to fund, approve or carry out the project. Under SEQR, the council is:
options: An involved agency
The lead agency
A reviewing agency
An interested agency
explanation: An interested agency lacks jurisdiction to fund, approve or undertake the action but participates because of its expertise or concern. An involved agency has that jurisdiction, and only an involved agency can serve as lead agency.

q: A town planning board schedules a hearing on a site plan for land 300 feet from the boundary of a neighboring village. Under GML §239-nn, the planning board must:
options: Notify the village clerk at least 10 days before the hearing
Get the village board's consent before approving the plan
Transfer the application to the village planning board
Let the village ZBA hold the hearing on the plan instead
explanation: For subdivisions, site plans, special use permits and use variances within 500 feet of an adjacent municipality, the hearing board must notify that municipality's clerk at least 10 days before the hearing. The neighbor may appear and be heard, but its consent is not required.

q: Under the Town Law, what is the minimum published notice for a ZBA variance hearing compared with a town board hearing on a zoning amendment?
options: 10 days for the ZBA and 5 days for the town board
5 days for the ZBA and 10 days for the town board
10 days for both the ZBA and the town board
5 days for both the ZBA and the town board
explanation: The ZBA must publish notice at least 5 days before the hearing and mail notice to the parties at least 5 days before; a town board zoning amendment needs at least 10 days' published notice, because §265 applies the §264 hearing-notice rules to amendments. Local laws may require more, such as mailing to neighbors.

q: A village planning board schedules its next meeting three weeks ahead. Under the Open Meetings Law, when must it give notice of the time and place to the news media and post it publicly?
options: At least 24 hours before the meeting
At least 10 days before the meeting
At least 72 hours before the meeting
At least 5 days before the meeting
explanation: For a meeting scheduled at least a week in advance, notice must go to the news media and be posted at least 72 hours beforehand (and on the website if the body has one). Meetings scheduled on shorter notice need notice at a reasonable time beforehand, to the extent practicable.

q: A village board wants to talk privately about a parcel it hopes to buy for a park, fearing public discussion would drive up the price. Under the Open Meetings Law, the board:
options: May never discuss real property outside a public session
May meet privately on any land matter if the mayor requests it
May meet privately only after the seller consents in writing
May enter executive session on a majority vote of its full membership
explanation: Executive session is allowed for a proposed purchase, sale or lease of real property when publicity would substantially affect its value. The motion must be made in an open meeting, name the general subject and pass by a majority of the total membership.

q: A town ZBA wants to deliberate on a contested use variance behind closed doors, arguing that it acts like a court. Under the Open Meetings Law:
options: Its deliberations must be open; the quasi-judicial exemption excludes ZBAs
It may deliberate privately, as long as it announces its vote publicly
It may deliberate privately, because quasi-judicial bodies are exempt
It may deliberate privately, but only if the applicant agrees to it
explanation: The Open Meetings Law exempts judicial and quasi-judicial proceedings, except proceedings of zoning boards of appeals. A ZBA's deliberations and vote must be held in public; voting publicly after private deliberation is the trap.

q: A salesperson files a Freedom of Information Law request with a town for the building permit file on a listing. Within what time must the town first respond, by granting, denying or acknowledging the request?
options: 72 hours
5 business days
14 calendar days
30 calendar days
explanation: Within 5 business days of receiving a FOIL request, an agency must make the records available, deny the request in writing, or acknowledge it with an approximate date for a response. 72 hours is the Open Meetings Law notice period, a different law.

q: A listing agent for a vacant lot sees the assessor's property class code for vacant residential land and wants to tell buyers what may be built. The most reliable source is:
options: The assessor's class code, which sets the permitted uses
The seller's account of what neighbors have built nearby
The current zoning law and map, confirmed with zoning officials
The tax receiver's bill, which shows the lot's legal use
explanation: Permitted uses come from the current zoning text and map, confirmed in writing with the zoning or building office. An assessor's class code describes how the parcel is classified for tax purposes and does not grant or limit development rights.
citation: Town Law §261 et seq.; Real Property Tax Law (property classification)

q: A buyer's agent is showing a Queens house advertised as a "three-family." The Department of Buildings records show a certificate of occupancy for a two-family dwelling. What is the most accurate conclusion?
options: The third unit is not a legal dwelling unit under the existing CO
The CO is outdated and the actual use controls for the sale
A three-family use is legal if the unit was rented over ten years
The third unit is legal once the seller registers it with HPD
explanation: The certificate of occupancy fixes the legal use and number of units; a unit beyond the CO is illegal until DOB approves an amended CO. Long rental history or HPD registration does not legalize occupancy, and lenders and title insurers often balk at the discrepancy.
citation: NYC Building Code / NYC Admin. Code Title 28 (certificate of occupancy); MDL §301

q: A Manhattan brownstone was completed in 1925 and has never had its use, egress, or number of units changed. The DOB has no certificate of occupancy on file. Which statement is correct?
options: The building is illegally occupied and must obtain a new CO before any sale
The seller must obtain a temporary CO from HPD before title can close
A CO is generally not required; a Letter of No Objection can confirm use
A CO must now be obtained because the building is being sold to a new owner
explanation: NYC buildings completed before 1938 generally do not need a CO unless there has been a change in use, egress, or occupancy; owners often obtain a DOB Letter of No Objection for lenders and buyers. A sale itself does not trigger a CO requirement, and HPD does not issue COs.
citation: NYC Department of Buildings certificate of occupancy rules (pre-1938 buildings)

q: A seller's title report shows an open ECB violation issued by the Department of Buildings. The seller says she already paid the penalty. What else is generally needed to resolve the violation on DOB records?
options: A release of the penalty recorded in ACRIS by the Department of Finance
Proof the condition was fixed, accepted by DOB as a certificate of correction
A dismissal letter from the local community board
Nothing; payment of the penalty closes the violation
explanation: Paying an ECB/OATH penalty settles the fine but does not cure the condition; the owner must certify correction to DOB before the violation is shown as resolved. Community boards have no enforcement role, and ACRIS records documents, not violation clearances.
citation: NYC Department of Buildings / OATH violation procedures

q: Summonses issued by the Department of Buildings, DEP, and the Fire Department for code violations are generally heard and decided by which body?
options: The Board of Standards and Appeals
The NYC Housing Court
The City Planning Commission
The OATH Hearings Division
explanation: OATH's Hearings Division (which absorbed the former Environmental Control Board) adjudicates summonses written by many city enforcement agencies. The BSA hears zoning variances and appeals of DOB determinations, not penalty summonses.

q: An owner of a six-unit Bronx building let his annual HPD multiple dwelling registration lapse. A tenant stops paying rent. What is the main legal consequence of the lapse?
options: The tenant's lease is automatically converted to a month-to-month term
The building's certificate of occupancy is suspended by DOB
The owner generally cannot bring a nonpayment proceeding until registered
The tenant may deduct any unpaid rent from the security deposit
explanation: Owners of multiple dwellings (3+ units) must register annually with HPD; an unregistered owner is barred from suing for nonpayment of rent until registration is current. The lapse does not affect the CO or change the lease term.
citation: NYC Housing Maintenance Code, Admin. Code §27-2097 and §27-2107

q: An HPD inspector cites a building for having no heat in January. Under the Housing Maintenance Code, this type of violation is classified as:
options: Class C, immediately hazardous
Class A, non-hazardous
Class B, hazardous
Class D, deferred maintenance
explanation: HPD classifies violations as A (non-hazardous), B (hazardous), or C (immediately hazardous); a lack of heat during heat season is a Class C condition requiring the fastest correction. There is no Class D.
citation: NYC Housing Maintenance Code, Admin. Code §27-2115

q: A buyer is purchasing a rowhouse in a New York City historic district and wants to add a rooftop addition visible from the street. What approval does the Landmarks Preservation Commission typically issue for work that affects protected exterior features?
options: A Certificate of No Effect
A Letter of No Objection
A temporary certificate of occupancy
A Certificate of Appropriateness
explanation: Work affecting significant protected features, such as a visible rooftop addition, requires an LPC Certificate of Appropriateness after review. A Certificate of No Effect covers DOB-permitted work that does not affect protected features; LNOs and TCOs are DOB documents.

q: An owner of an apartment in a designated landmark building wants to gut-renovate the kitchen. The work needs a DOB permit but does not touch any protected exterior or interior features. What LPC document is typically issued?
options: A Certificate of Appropriateness
A Certificate of No Effect
A use variance
A zoning special permit
explanation: LPC issues a Certificate of No Effect when work requiring a DOB permit will not affect protected architectural features. A Certificate of Appropriateness is for work that does affect them; variances and special permits are zoning tools, not LPC approvals.

q: A seller boasts that his private apartment's ornate living room could be designated an "interior landmark." Why is that claim unlikely to be true?
options: Interior landmarks must be customarily open or accessible to the public
Interior landmarks must be located in buildings over 100 years old
Only the City Council, not LPC, may designate any interior
Interiors can be designated only in city-owned buildings
explanation: The Landmarks Law limits interior landmarks to interiors customarily open or accessible to the public, such as lobbies and theaters, so a private apartment interior does not qualify. LPC, not the Council alone, designates, and there is no 100-year or city-ownership rule.

q: A buyer's attorney orders municipal searches and finds unpaid water and sewer charges billed by the Department of Environmental Protection. Why does this matter for the sale?
options: Water charges are personal debts that never affect title
DEP charges are paid only by tenants, not by owners
Unpaid water and sewer charges can become a lien on the property
The charges must be appealed to the City Planning Commission
explanation: NYC water and sewer charges are a lien on the property, like real estate taxes, and can even be sold in the tax lien sale; they are typically paid or escrowed at closing. They are not merely personal debts and are not a CPC matter.
citation: NYC Admin. Code §11-301 and Title 11, ch. 3 (water and sewer charges)

q: Each January, NYC owners receive a notice showing the city's estimate of their property's market value and assessed value for the coming tax year. This notice comes from:
options: The Department of City Planning
The Department of Finance
The Department of Buildings
The Office of the Borough President
explanation: The Department of Finance values and assesses NYC property and mails the annual Notice of Property Value each January. DCP handles planning and zoning, DOB handles construction, and borough presidents have no assessment role.
citation: NYC Charter ch. 11 (Department of Finance); RPTL Article 18

q: A Brooklyn homeowner asks who decides her property tax rate. Which statement about New York City is accurate?
options: Finance both assesses the property and sets the tax rates
The borough president sets a separate tax rate for each borough
The City Planning Commission sets the tax rates by zoning district
Finance assesses the property; the City Council sets the tax rates
explanation: The Department of Finance determines market and assessed values, while the City Council adopts the budget and fixes the tax rates for each tax class. Borough presidents and the CPC have no rate-setting power.
citation: NYC Charter (City Council budget and tax-fixing powers); RPTL Article 18

q: A buyer's agent wants to look up the recorded deed and mortgage history of a Bronx property online. Which Department of Finance system holds these records?
options: ZoLa
BIS
ACRIS
HPD Online
explanation: ACRIS (Automated City Register Information System) is the Department of Finance's City Register system for recording and searching deeds and mortgages. ZoLa is DCP's zoning map tool, BIS is DOB's buildings database, and HPD Online shows housing-code data.
citation: NYC Office of the City Register (Department of Finance); RPL §291

q: Which of the following is NOT a role of a New York City borough president?
options: Granting zoning variances for lots in the borough
Appointing members of the community boards in the borough
Issuing an advisory recommendation during ULURP
Appointing one member of the City Planning Commission
explanation: Borough presidents appoint community board members, appoint one CPC member each, and issue advisory ULURP recommendations. Zoning variances for individual lots are granted by the Board of Standards and Appeals, not the borough president.

q: How are members of a New York City community board selected?
options: Elected by the voters of the community district for staggered four-year terms
Appointed by the mayor, subject to the advice and consent of the City Council
Chosen by the City Planning Commission from a pool of local applicants
Appointed by the borough president, at least half nominated by local council members
explanation: Community board members (up to 50, unpaid, serving staggered two-year terms) are appointed by the borough president, and at least half must come from nominees of the City Council members who represent the district. They are not elected and are not mayoral or CPC appointees.

q: How is the 13-member City Planning Commission composed?
options: Thirteen members elected citywide on a nonpartisan ballot every four years
Seven mayoral appointees, one per borough president, and one public advocate pick
All thirteen appointed by the City Council speaker with full Council consent
The five borough presidents plus eight community board chairs serving ex officio
explanation: The mayor appoints seven members, including the chair (who also directs the Department of City Planning); each of the five borough presidents appoints one; and the public advocate appoints one. 7 + 5 + 1 = 13.

q: Before a private rezoning application can begin the formal ULURP clock, which agency reviews it and certifies it as complete?
options: The Department of City Planning
The Board of Standards and Appeals
The Department of Buildings
The local community board
explanation: The Department of City Planning, staff to the CPC, reviews ULURP applications and certifies them complete, which starts the formal review timeline. The community board's 60-day review begins only after certification.

q: A DOB plan examiner rules that a proposed rear yard extension violates the Zoning Resolution. The owner believes the examiner misread the rule. After exhausting DOB review, where does the owner appeal the determination?
options: The City Planning Commission
The Landmarks Preservation Commission
The Board of Standards and Appeals
The OATH Hearings Division
explanation: The BSA hears appeals from DOB decisions interpreting the Zoning Resolution and the building codes, much as a zoning board of appeals does outside NYC. The CPC makes zoning policy and map changes; it does not hear appeals of individual permit denials.

q: To grant a variance under the NYC Zoning Resolution, the Board of Standards and Appeals must make several findings. Which situation would most likely defeat the application?
options: The lot has an unusually irregular shape
The owner's own lot split created the hardship
Strict compliance would prevent a reasonable return
The request is the minimum relief necessary
explanation: BSA variance findings include unique physical conditions, no reasonable return under strict compliance, no harm to neighborhood character, a hardship not created by the owner or a predecessor in title, and minimum variance. A self-created hardship defeats the application; the other choices support it.

q: An owner seeks a BSA variance for a single lot in Brooklyn. Which statement about the review process is correct?
options: It must go through every ULURP stage, ending with a binding City Council vote
It needs only Department of Buildings approval, with no hearing
It requires a borough-wide referendum after the BSA votes
It is not a ULURP action, but the community board gets notice and may comment
explanation: BSA variances and special permits follow the BSA's own procedure with a public hearing and community board notice, not ULURP. ULURP covers actions such as zoning map changes and CPC special permits; there is no referendum.

q: The City wants to amend the text of the Zoning Resolution citywide, without changing any district boundaries on the zoning map. Which statement is accurate?
options: Text amendments follow ULURP exactly, starting with each community board
Text amendments take effect on a CPC vote, with no Council role
Text amendments are not ULURP actions, but CPC and Council review still apply
Text amendments are decided by the Board of Standards and Appeals
explanation: Zoning text amendments are governed by Charter §§200–201, not ULURP: they are referred for community and borough comment, require CPC approval, and are then automatically subject to City Council review under §197-d. Zoning map amendments, by contrast, are ULURP actions.

q: Counting only the four sequential ULURP review periods after certification (community board, borough president, City Planning Commission, City Council), what is the maximum total time?
options: 200 days
150 days
215 days
240 days
explanation: 60 (community board) + 30 (borough president) + 60 (CPC) + 50 (City Council) = 200 days. 150 omits the Council's 50 days; 215 adds the 5-day mayoral veto and 10-day override periods; 240 wrongly assumes 60 days for each stage.

q: Under ULURP, the City Council approves a rezoning and the mayor vetoes it. What can the Council do?
options: Override the veto by a simple majority of members present
Send the rezoning to the borough president for a final vote
Nothing; a mayoral veto of a land use action is final
Override the veto by a two-thirds vote of all members
explanation: Council land use actions are final unless the mayor files a disapproval within 5 days. The Council may override within 10 days by a two-thirds vote of all its members; a simple majority is not enough. This rule applies to an ordinary rezoning. Since the 2025 Charter amendments, qualifying affordable-housing applications instead go to the Affordable Housing Appeals Board, which replaces the veto and override for those applications.

q: A Brooklyn lot measures 25 feet by 100 feet in a district with a maximum floor area ratio (FAR) of 3.0. The existing building contains 5,500 square feet of floor area. How much unused floor area ("air rights") remains?
options: 7,500 sq ft
2,000 sq ft
2,500 sq ft
1,833 sq ft
explanation: Lot area = 25 × 100 = 2,500 sq ft. Maximum floor area = 2,500 × 3.0 = 7,500 sq ft. Unused = 7,500 − 5,500 = 2,000 sq ft. 7,500 forgets the existing building; 2,500 is just the lot area; 1,833 wrongly divides 5,500 by 3.

q: A buyer wants to open a small grocery on the ground floor of a building in a residence (R) district in New York City. On the zoning map, the block is shaded with a C2 designation. What does this indicate?
options: A commercial overlay allowing local retail within the residence district
A manufacturing district in which new housing is generally prohibited
A special historic district placed under LPC design jurisdiction
A conservation area where new construction is barred entirely
explanation: NYC's Zoning Resolution has three basic district types: residence (R), commercial (C), and manufacturing (M). C1 and C2 overlays mapped within residence districts allow local retail and services, typically on the ground floor. Overlays are zoning, not landmark, designations.
citation: NYC Zoning Resolution Article III (commercial overlay districts)

q: A buyer is purchasing a Bronx building that has lawfully housed a non-conforming auto repair shop, but the shop has been closed for three continuous years. Under the NYC Zoning Resolution, the buyer generally:
options: May resume the use because non-conforming status runs with the land forever
May resume the use after paying a fee to the Department of Finance
Cannot resume the non-conforming use after a two-year discontinuance
Needs only a new DOB permit to reopen the repair shop
explanation: ZR §52-61 provides that once substantially all of a non-conforming use is discontinued for a continuous two-year period, the property may thereafter be used only for a conforming use, regardless of intent to resume. Since 2024 (City of Yes for Economic Opportunity), vacant ground-floor storefronts in residential buildings in R districts may be reactivated with local retail or office uses, but that exception does not revive an auto repair shop.

q: A buyer is considering an apartment in a 12-story Manhattan co-op. Which Department of Buildings program requires periodic inspection of the building's exterior walls, a possible source of special assessments?
options: The Multiple Dwelling Registration, every year
The Facade Inspection Safety Program, every five years
The Uniform Land Use Review Procedure, every ten years
The Notice of Property Value review, every January
explanation: DOB's Facade Inspection Safety Program (Local Law 11) requires buildings taller than six stories to have their facades inspected every five years, and repairs can be costly for owners and shareholders. Registration is an HPD matter; ULURP and the NOPV are unrelated.

q: An investor is buying a 60,000-square-foot Manhattan office building. Which NYC law sets greenhouse gas emissions limits for most buildings over 25,000 square feet, with penalties for exceeding them?
options: Local Law 11
The FARE Act
Local Law 1 of 2004
Local Law 97
explanation: Local Law 97 imposes carbon emissions caps, administered by DOB, on most buildings over 25,000 gross square feet, so a buyer should review compliance and potential penalties. Local Law 11 is facade inspection, the FARE Act concerns broker fees, and Local Law 1 of 2004 concerns lead paint.
citation: NYC Admin. Code Title 28, Article 320 (Local Law 97 of 2019)

q: A landlord rents lofts as apartments in a multiple dwelling that has no residential certificate of occupancy. A tenant stops paying rent. Under the Multiple Dwelling Law, the landlord generally:
options: May collect double rent as a penalty for the tenant's default
May evict the tenant without a court proceeding
May be barred from recovering rent while the CO violation continues
May recover the rent once HPD approves the lease
explanation: Multiple Dwelling Law §302 bars an owner from recovering rent, or maintaining a nonpayment proceeding, for a period during which a multiple dwelling is occupied in violation of the CO requirement of §301 (Loft Law interim multiple dwellings in compliance are a statutory exception). Self-help eviction is unlawful in NY, and HPD does not approve leases.
